extracted.intended_audience: founders and PR/communications people at tech startups pitching tech reporters and newsletter writers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for how tech startups should craft pitches and press releases to get coverage from beat reporters and newsletter writers; includes what journalists look for, common founder mistakes, and newsletter-specific best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real product change (not a rebrand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Real product change, not a rebrand
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters prioritize substantive product changes over cosmetic rebrands — the news should reflect an actual change in product or offering, not mere renaming or repositioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiable numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers I can verify (DAU, revenue, growth rate)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete metrics that a reporter can check or corroborate (e.g., daily active users, revenue, growth rate). Avoid vague or inflated figures that can't be substantiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source close to the decision / founder-level source
rubrics_metrics.description: Source close to the decision (founder, not PR rep)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary source should be someone directly involved in the decision (preferably the founder). Journalists prefer speaking with people who have direct knowledge rather than intermediaries or PR reps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / exclusivity of story
rubrics_metrics.description: Story I haven't seen elsewhere this week; Best releases are ones I never see — exclusive given to ONE outlet
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists value novelty — don't pitch widely distributed or already-covered stories. Offering an exclusive to a single outlet increases the chance of pickup; wire distribution is less effective initially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Villain or stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: A villain or stakes (regulatory, competitive)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good stories often have a clear antagonist or stakes (e.g., regulatory pressure, competitive threat) that create conflict and make the piece interesting and reportable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat relevance / affects the reporter's beat
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this affect platforms (the beat I cover)?; Beat-relevant angle
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitches should clearly connect to the reporter's beat and explain why the news matters to that coverage area (e.g., platform-level implications). If it doesn't affect the beat, it's unlikely to get traction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and newsworthiness (followups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Will this generate followups in 6 months?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters favor stories that are not one-off promotional items but that can produce follow-up reporting and ongoing relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advances an ongoing story
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it advance a story I'm already telling?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the pitch ties into narratives the reporter is already tracking, it's more likely to be covered. Show how the news connects to existing threads or previous reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term source potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the source going to be a long-term contact?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists value sources who can provide ongoing information. Position the contact as someone who will be available and useful beyond a single story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid investor-style pitches
rubrics_metrics.description: They write to journalists like they're talking to investors
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: founders often pitch using investor-focused language (TAM, traction) which is less useful for reporters. Instead, emphasize concrete product details and news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive TAM/traction focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Too much TAM/traction talk, not enough product
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters want product-focused details and news hooks rather than broad market-size or traction narratives; minimize TAM-heavy framing in pitches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't optimize solely for 'getting covered'
rubrics_metrics.description: They optimize for "getting covered" instead of telling a true story
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: crafting pitches that try to game coverage rather than honestly describing the news reduces credibility and interest. Tell a true, reportable story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not send releases before product actually works
rubrics_metrics.description: They send the release before the product actually works
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid announcing or pitching things that are not functional or demonstrable; premature announcements erode trust and invite criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire-distributed releases are mostly ignored
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire-distributed releases mostly ignored
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution via wire services without personalization tends to have low pickup among beat reporters and newsletter writers; prioritize targeted outreach and exclusives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalized email with embargo
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalized email with embargo gets read
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send a short, personalized pitch email and offer an embargo if appropriate — this approach is more likely to get a reporter's attention than mass distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire after exclusive for SEO
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire after exclusive runs is fine for SEO
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to run the wire release after an exclusive outlet has published; use the wire post-publication for broader visibility and SEO rather than primary outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsletter writers are pickier than reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsletter writers are pickier than reporters
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substack/newsletter writers often have higher editorial standards for relevance and substance; they avoid overtly promotional pieces and expect a clear, interesting angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need substantive, not promotional items for newsletters
rubrics_metrics.description: Want substantive, not promotional, items; Will not run "look how cool this company is" pieces
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsletter pitches should provide real reporting or substantive news, not puff pieces. Avoid pitches that read like marketing copy praising the company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrarian or counter-intuitive frame for newsletters
rubrics_metrics.description: Always need a contrarian or counter-intuitive frame
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To stand out in newsletters, frame the story with a contrarian or surprising angle that challenges expectations and invites reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community reactions matter (comments will roast weak items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments section will roast weak items mercilessly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weak or promotional pieces are exposed by readers; expect community scrutiny for newsletter placements and ensure the story can withstand close public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject line should state the news (not the company)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject line must include the news, not the company
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the subject line to communicate the news hook succinctly (what happened) rather than just naming the company; this increases open/read rates among journalists and newsletter editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep pitch body short (under 150 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Body under 150 words
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the pitch concise — under ~150 words — focusing on the news, the key facts, and availability for comment or demo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include product links, screenshots, demo video
rubrics_metrics.description: Link to product, screenshots, demo video
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide direct links to the product and visual/demo assets so reporters can quickly evaluate and verify claims; make the news demonstrable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founder availability for quick call
rubrics_metrics.description: Make founder available for 15-min call same day
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer quick access to a founder or knowledgeable executive (e.g., 15-minute same-day call) to facilitate reporting and get questions answered promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demoable / screenshottable content
rubrics_metrics.description: Demoable / screenshottable
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that can be demonstrated or screenshotted are more attractive to reporters and newsletter writers because they provide tangible evidence and visuals for the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality rubric summary (newsletter journalist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive product/decision news; Verifiable numbers; Founder-level source; Beat-relevant angle; Exclusive offered, not blasted; Demoable / screenshottable
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compact checklist journalists use to judge pitches: substantive product or decision news, verifiable metrics, direct founder/source access, clear beat relevance, preference for exclusives, and demonstrable visuals/demos.
